newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland's "doomsday book" row hots ups.
newsitem.headline: Ireland's "doomsday book" row hots ups.

text.p: A "doomsday book" of payments to Irish politicians by a department store chain will be handed over to parliament this week, opening a new chapter on a row which has already forced one government minister to resign.

Prime Minister John Bruton's government said in a weekend statement that it had reached agreement with the Dunnes Store chain that the list of payments would be handed to the Government Secretary unopened.

It will then be given to a retired judge who will examine it and extract the names of politicians and public officers who took money from Dunnes, a multi-million pound chain whose shops dominate the High Street of every major Irish town.
The names will then be given to parliament's commitee on procedures and privileges which will decide whether anyone has a case to answer.

Those names are expected to include the mysterious former senior government official who is reported by the media to have received one million pounds from Dunnes for unspecified purposes in the 1990s.

Former Prime Minister Charles Haughey, one of the political giants of modern Irish political life, has denied ever taking money from Dunnes or being involved in a British bank account through which the cash was handled.
The Examiner newspaper quoted a source close to Haughey as denying receiving any money from Dunnes. The newspaper said Haughey, of the Fianna Fail party, was seeking legal advice.
Political sources said names on the list could become public this week as parliament begins counting down to a Christmas holiday recess and the Irish budget early next year.

The budget is widely expected to feature substantial tax cuts to sweeten the government's public standing before a general election which is due by November next year but could be held early in the spring, the sources said.

The controversy erupted one week ago when Michael Lowry, a rising star in Bruton's Fine Gael party, resigned after admitting a newspaper report that Dunnes paid for the 200,000 pound ($320,000) rennovation of his private home.

Bruton's Fine Gael party later admitted that it too had taken cash from Dunnes in the 1990s to clear its debts, sparking a fierce debate about the funding of politics and links between political parties and big business.
At present political parties are funded by a mixture of government grant and private donation.

"If we're going to clean up the whole thing and make sure that there is no impropriety, we're going to have to have some mechanism for funding elections in this country," Fianna Fail Senator Dick Roche said in weekened remarks.
"We're going to destroy politics in this country by our collective failure to resolve the issue of funding. There's a degree of cowardice out there," he said.
Senior Irish political figures speculated that the list might estabish links between politicians, business and developers which a cynical the public has long suspected.
Ireland has been transformed over the past decade with huge inflows of European Union cash and its economy is now growing faster than most in the 15-nation bloc.
